translations.text: Yesterday’s discourse on the body amazed us. It explained the beauty of nature and marveled at the wisdom of the master builder. For when nature is explained, the Creator is glorified, and when the work is praised, it brings honor to the craftsman. But while we were occupied with this, the time for the rites of evening worship came upon us. While the lamp of the body was being proclaimed, the evening lamp was brought forward for the service of the church. Along with that lamp, he added a mention of a third lamp, the divine commandments. The first lamp, that of the body, has the testimony of the Life-giver himself: “The eye is the lamp of the body.” The lamp made from fire is known to everyone through experience and custom. And the third lamp is proclaimed by David, who says, “Your words are a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” But today the teaching of our revered father, the father of us all, showed us yet another lamp, the lamp of the Gospel: a lamp that does not rise in opposition to the sun, but is obedient to the Sun of righteousness. Christ comes to be baptized, and John baptizes him, not puffed up with arrogant pride, but serving the divine command. A man who himself needed baptism baptized the Baptizer and Lord of all, approaching him not presumptuously, but in obedience to the command. John is a lamp who bears in himself the pattern of the saints of the Old Testament. Just as the laws of the Jews were called a lamp, so those who lived virtuously according to the laws were also called lamps.

Pay attention, I beg you. John was a lamp, for the Law and the Prophets were until John. David was a lamp, for when, in his old age, he boldly sought to go out to battle against Zabron, the elders of the people restrained him and would not let him go to battle. They all raised a protest, saying, “Do not go to battle, lest you extinguish the lamp of Israel.” David was a lamp; John was a lamp. But once the true light and the Sun of Righteousness rose and sent out its brilliant, clear rays from heaven, those who grow in virtue through that light surpass—surpass the lamps. Those men bore the name of a lamp because they had served under the Law, which was called a lamp. But these, illuminated by the light of the gospel, who live according to it and display that same manner of life, have passed beyond the rank of a lamp and are called light. Although a lamp is also light, what comparison can it have with the light itself? And whatever the order of nature bestowed, the King’s generosity granted to the disciples.

And see Christ’s love for humanity: he made the disciples share in the very name he gave himself. “I am,” he says, “the light of the world,” and elsewhere, “You are the light of the world.” What new graces and gifts, surpassing all words and thoughts! See how his love for humanity overcomes the order of nature. The sun rises—and why do I say that the sun rises? Even when it sends out its forerunner, the dawn in the east, it puts all the hosts of stars to flight, and all the stars hide and conceal themselves. It is not that they perish, but that they are hidden by the surpassing light of the sun. But Jesus, the Sun of Righteousness, who rose after the former night, not only illuminated like stars those prophets who already shone at his coming, but also gathered other lights to himself. Along with the Sun of Righteousness rose lights, preachers of the truth, marshals of the ranks of godliness. Of these Paul says, “Among them you are to appear as lights in the world, holding the word of life, so that I may boast on the day of Christ.”

Have you seen the rays of the Sun of Righteousness? See also the evangelist, how he sets down names that are above all rhetorical names, above all vain philosophy, above those of grammarians and practitioners of the arts, and even above every title of honor and distinction—the names of the sons. What does this mean? Rustic names and heavenly minds accomplish great deeds. Bartholomew and Thaddeus are names foreign to the Greek language, yet they cast away all [?] and plant complete knowledge in its place. The giver of life chose fishermen, not to reject the wise in any way, nor to dishonor the eloquent, but to keep the beginning of the preaching free from suspicion. The word is preached through fishermen so that the power of the one who accomplishes the work may be made clear. We do not marvel because they are fishermen, but because through fishermen the power that is above the world was proclaimed.

God could have stirred eloquent speakers to defend the preaching, so that the wisdom of the knowledge of God might be revealed. But he did not wish to make the truth of the cross ineffective. That is why Paul said, “I did not come with superiority of speech, lest the cross of Christ be made ineffective”—that is, lest it be considered something pointless and rejected through arguments. Instead, the power of the crucified one planted the church through the company of the apostles. He planted the word of truth through untrained tongues, which had been schooled only in the divine laws. And after planting it through them, he then watered it through the wise as well. He did not do this without a purpose: those who make excuses for their sins must not be able to say, “He deceived the ignorant, but could not persuade the wise and the powerful.” Rather, to confront those whose minds were bent on deception, he made the fishermen eloquent—the simple, the unlearned, and the incapable. For this reason, though not together with them, God raised up articulate, eloquent preachers even in the apostles’ own time. “A certain man,” it says, “an Alexandrian named Apollos, a Jew by birth, came to Ephesus. He was articulate and mighty in the Scriptures and in understanding, and eloquent in exposition.” “Mighty,” it says, “in the Scriptures.” And what skill did he possess? He gave much help to those who had believed. “In public,” it says, “he refuted the Jews.” Do you see the sword of Christ, how it is sharpened through everyone? He trains the fishermen and arms the wise. And since eloquence serves error, he often strips evil of its weapon and clothes virtue with it. Error is clothed in reasoned arguments; truth seizes them and kills error with those very arguments. So too, when the blessed David brought down the giant Goliath, he first struck him with his own weapons, and then cut off his head with that foreigner’s sword. Taking it from him, he beheaded him with it. In the same way, truth knows how to draw the sword of error and kill error itself with it. There were wise men among the Gentiles; Christ sent out against them champions from among the zealous Jews. Among the Jewish people there was a sword of steel: Saul, who in his error opposed the churches and cut and [?] the faith of Christ. The life-giver took that same sword and placed it in the church’s hands, to drive away every evil that might rise against it. This is precisely what the blessed David said: “Sinners drew their swords and bent their bows. Their swords will enter their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.”

God spoke through the wise, and he also spoke through the ignorant, so that he might show his power through both: through fishermen, so that with untrained tongues he might reject the skill of empty rhetoric; and through the wise, so that with profound knowledge he might unravel subtle deceit. And by building a wall around the faith, he might strengthen humanity. What he accomplished among the ignorant and the eloquent, he also accomplished among kings. Listen to how this happened. The Giver of Life could have brought kings into obedience to the preaching at the very beginning of its proclamation, at the first opportunity, and raised them up as allies of the worship of God, as they are now. But he did not do so, lest he bring the truth under suspicion, as though the Church had been established by human protection and not by the power of God. He stripped it of human assistance and clothed it with heavenly power. Until the most devout Constantine, thirty-five emperors ruled the Romans, one after another, and they were unwilling to submit to the faith. This was so that it might be learned that grace does not borrow any human power, but possesses its own power inherently. And because he saw the whole world in error, lest those who devise excuses for sins should again say, ‘He was able to deceive the ignorant and the unsuspecting, but he could not ensnare kings and rulers,’ he sets the word ablaze, brings kings under the yoke of the worship of God, and leads all [?] into a single unity of truth. Thus it might become evident that the King of kings and Lord of lords showed the surpassing greatness of heavenly wisdom through humble preaching.

Today the names of the apostles were read out, the fishermen were proclaimed, and the words of the unlearned were made known—those who offered every instruction to the world. And pay attention to [?]. ‘The first of the twelve,’ it says, ‘was Simon, who was called Peter,’ the rock of the Church, the foundation of the worship of God. He had the name Simon from his father and mother, but he was named Peter by the Giver of Life. ‘You are Peter,’ he says—which means ‘rock’—‘and on this rock I will build my Church.’ All the Church’s preaching stands established upon rock, and every heretical error upon unstable clay. The firm rock that holds the building up is one thing, and the unstable earth that will not remain steady for the builders is another. Indeed, it does not even remain steady in itself. Their statements are unstable, their words are cold, and their beliefs deserve reproach, because human thoughts have been mixed into the faith of God. The clay strives to shake the rock, but the rock is not overcome. ‘The gates of hell,’ he says, ‘will not terrify it.’

The disciples of the schismatics are like potters who mold bricks. For they remedy the weakness of the clay with some straw, and thus make what is loose harder, and what is fragile appears solid. It appears solid until something harmful comes upon it. But if rain or a flood or [?] or anything else strikes it, it cannot withstand it. Therefore the prophet speaks to those who trust in earthly things and suppose that nothing bad will come from them: “Thus says the Lord: Go down into the clay, tread it with straw, and make yourself harder than brick, and fire will devour you.” He rebukes those who trust in bodily and earthly things and consider their strength invincible. The foundation of the Church is the rock, and that of the schismatics is Jerusalem. The prophet wished to show—or rather, God himself through the prophet—what the Church established upon the rock is like, and what this Jewish fold is like, which does not remain stable and firm. He says to the prophet Ezekiel, “Take a brick for me, engrave Jerusalem on it, and surround it with a siege rampart.” Why a brick? So that you may learn the nature of brick and of rock. Jerusalem stood upon brick, but the foundation of the Church is the rock. Indeed, even if we call the Church a rock, we do not lie; nor do I deny the rock upon which it stands. The Church too is a rock, for it has Christ as its firm rock, and another rock, Peter, who received that name through his confession. “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

But I wish to make this clear: why did John the Evangelist, who was so abundantly endowed that he gathered the showers of the Gospel into himself—the son of thunder, who drew the entire abundance of grace into himself all at once—not adopt Peter’s wording at the beginning of his Gospel? He did not say, “In the beginning was the Son,” nor, “In the beginning was the Only-begotten.” Instead, leaving aside the names “Son” and “Only-begotten,” he turned to “Word”: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Peter was pronounced blessed not because he called him “Word,” but because he confessed him as “Son.” Why, then, did blessed John leave that blessing behind and turn to “Word”? The apostles knew what they were preaching, but those who were to receive it from them could not bear the loftiness of their words. For at the beginning, the preaching and the word rang out in both worthy and unworthy ears. So that they would not defile the divine teaching with human ideas—hearing “Son” and imagining a father and mother, material substance, and the other needs of the body—he therefore turned to the name “Word,” which could make clear his freedom from suffering at the very beginning of his utterance. And see what order he follows: he set up a ladder and leads us through many distinct stages to the name “Son” at the top—not because he denied it, but because he reserves it for the appropriate time.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word,” so that you may learn that his birth is unforced and has freedom as its own characteristic; for the mind is always the father of a word. “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” Indeed, he would not even be called “Word” by himself if he were not someone’s word. And whose Word would he be? He was, he says, in the beginning with God, and the Word was God. First he explains the unforced birth, and then he shows that, while having his own person, he is inseparable from the Father, united with him in nature, will, and activity. “And the Word was God.” By this he declares his honor twice over. And the point established beforehand is that what is needed is not an arrangement of words, but confirmation of realities. “In the beginning was the Word” makes his unforced birth clear. “And the Word was God” shows the inseparable unity. “And the Word was God” shows his undiminished honor. “He was in the beginning with God.” He repeats this to establish the same meaning firmly. And because he called him “Word,” while the words we use do not adequately reveal the manner of the things being discussed, he sets out the statement more clearly and shows him to be at once God, Word, and Creator: “And everything came into being through him.”

And in this the heretics find something of a remedy. “He said ‘through him,’” they say, “and not ‘by him’ or ‘from him,’ but ‘through him.’ But I would like to learn with certainty from those who have stumbled, who do not know their own nature and yet stumble into such errors, and who investigate and examine that nature which surpasses every understanding. What difference do they suppose there is between ‘through him’ and ‘from him’? For we must not give a judgment at random, but show its confirmation from the holy Scriptures.

What does “through him” mean? “The Father,” they say, “made things through him.” They take refuge in that particular expression as in a fence [?], and employ it as a shelter for their own evils, bringing forward the statement, “The Father made things through him.” Tell me how, and do not merely bring forward the expression in a confused jumble. I cannot understand an expression empty of meaning, for I am ignorant. When things are done among us “through someone,” it is possible to understand the circumstances: a master acts through a servant; one gives an order, and the other carries it out. A master acts through a craftsman; one sets out the design, and the other constructs the work. Now tell me how: how does he act through the Son? Does he give an order as a master to a servant? Or does he, like someone unskilled, go to a skilled worker? Or does he, like a craftsman, carry out the work with an adze, a saw, or some other tool? Whatever manner you wish to propose, make clear what you understand, so that I may learn what I believe. Did he give orders as a master to a servant? Or, like someone unskilled, did he give the work to a craftsman to do? Or, like a craftsman, did he work with a tool? Come, tell me which manner you suppose it to be.

“Like a father,” he says, “through a son.” You have not yet made clear what I want, for I am not asking about the identity of the speaker or the hearer, or the appearance of the one giving the command and the manner of the one receiving it. They say that the Father commanded and the Son acted. Show me how the Son created and how the Father gave commands. They say that the Father gave a command by a word and the Son acted. In what manner? Did he act by putting his hand to work? That would indicate that he underwent bodily toil, if he performed some such action. “No,” they say, “he himself created by a word.” See how their wickedness multiplies! Tell me the utterance that the Father spoke; set before me the word by which the Son created. But so that I do not allow you to [?] and say whatever you wish, I will, whether you wish it or not, [?] you into divine teaching and show you the Creator’s utterances. God said, “Let there be light.” God said, “Let there be a firmament.” Who was it who spoke? Immediately they retort that the Father spoke and the Son carried out the command. If these were words of someone giving a command, God would not have said, “Let there be light,” but “Make the light”; and the Son would have heard and made it. But tell me, please: why is the same utterance found in both cases—“God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” and again, “God said, ‘Let there be a firmament,’ and there was a firmament”? If the Father employed that utterance, “Let there be light” and “Let there be a firmament,” why did that same utterance not take effect and accomplish the work, but instead require another utterance? This is a weighty argument. Write down that the Father spoke, as the heretics say, and the Son stood nearby and heard what God said, “Let there be light,” and that the Son received the utterance and made the light. Could those frenzied minds be so presumptuous as to say that the Word of God underwent bodily activity and toil? And if they persist in speaking of bodily activity rather than divine power, David comes forward and rebukes them: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”

Now, if the Father said, “Let there be light,” and the utterance that went forth accomplished no work but waited for the Son, was the Father lacking something, and did he make up for his lack through the Son? He said, “Let there be light,” and nature did not accompany it. He said, “Let there be a firmament,” and the word accomplished no work. Rather, the Father spoke and waited for the Son’s act of creation. See what you are doing! Perhaps, while trying to be clever about this, you will introduce another impiety: that the Father was somehow weak and the Son powerful.

Come, tell me: explain the manner—what does “through the Son” mean? “Through the Son,” they say, “he made the creatures.” Who made him? “The Father made him.” May Christ forgive these monstrous sins! For even the words make me shudder when I hear this account of blasphemy. And do not be surprised at this: when he was about to introduce the blasphemy of the heretics, he did not introduce it in explicit words, but exercised caution. He did not state the blasphemy openly, but under a pretext. Thus he even said to God, “Go on, touch his flesh, and see whether he will not bless you to your face,” instead of saying, “May you be cursed.” The disciples of the heretics say this; let it be heard as coming from them, and not from us. “The Father,” they say, “made only the Son, and the Son made all the other creatures.” Explain the manner of his coming into being. If the Son came into being by an act of will, we too came into being by God’s will, as did the other creatures. What difference will there be between those who worship and the one who receives worship? If he came into being in the same way as I did, why should he demand worship from me? If he came into being out of nothing by God’s will, and the world came into being out of nothing by God’s will, I do not see what difference there will be between them. If God the Father [?] him in between, and the Son the other creatures—if there is any distinction between them in the way the Son came into being, explain it. But if there is none, and the Son came into being out of nothing solely by an act of will, and all the other creatures came into being out of nothing by an act of will, how can one who came into being out of nothing by God’s will, just as we did, receive worship from us?

“Yes,” they say, “he receives it, because he is not like the other creatures: he surpasses all creatures and surpasses every rank of things that have come into being.” They are clever only with words, and they dishonor his nature. It is not because he is above the creatures that he ought to receive worship from the creatures, unless he is the Creator and Lord of the creatures, and [?] from nonexistence. For a creature does not receive worship from creatures. The heavens are greater than the earth, but the earth does not owe worship to the heavens. The stars are greater than plants, but plants do not bow down to the stars. An angel is greater than a human being, but a human being does not bow down to an angel. And why should I even speak of human nature? What resemblance does an ant bear to Gabriel, or a gnat to Michael? Yet because those are creatures and these are creatures, in the matter of worship the angels descend to the level of these, and these fallen creatures rise to the level of the angels, and they form a crown of worship around the throne. In their superiority, the angels are separated and set apart from these creatures; but in being created and in worship, they are close and near to one another.

And listen to blessed David: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” he says, “praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts: sun and moon, all stars and light, the heaven of heavens, and the waters above the heavens.” When he has finished listing those who are above the world, he adds to the same passage, “Praise the Lord from the earth.” With the same words he prescribes the same worship. Angels do not worship in one way and human beings in another. “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” he says, “praise the Lord from the earth. Praise him, all his angels, dragons and all the depths.” What likeness could there be between angels and dragons? “Fire and hail, snow and ice, wind and storm, wild beasts and all livestock”: bears, lions, leopards, panthers, boars, and all wild beasts; livestock—camels, donkeys, oxen. All these worship together with them, not considering the superiority of their rank, but recognizing the shared honor of worship. “Wild beasts,” he says, “and all livestock, creeping things and birds”: ravens praise together with angels. “Creeping things,” he says: vipers, snakes, scorpions, and every kind of creeping thing. Do you see that superiority in honor does not diminish the worship of those who are lower? For it is not the case that, because those are higher creatures, these have no share in worship. Rather, the Lord’s honor and the divine being are to be glorified by all, for all creatures owe worship to the Creator. But now show the difference that lies between them. When you say of the Father that everything is from him, you indicate his superiority by your gestures alone, without speaking. For even before their words, the heretics blaspheme with their faces. When they argue about the Father, they begin to say, “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” Before your tongue speaks, your face blasphemes; before your words, your expression belittles him. Oh, the ingratitude! The prophets magnify even created things, while the heretics belittle the Creator. David honors and exalts created things: “How great are your works, Lord!” Those who worship God magnify even his works, while the impious belittle even the Creator.

“They magnify created things,” they say, “because these have no greatness of their own. But the Son must not be magnified beyond what he is; his honor must be kept within a certain limit”—as though they had the authority to pity the Son and show him kindness. They speak impiously; they act impiously, not understanding the meaning of their words. But I know that Christ is magnified, not by any addition to his nature, but by the gratitude of those who worship him. Listen to blessed David as he magnifies him: “I will bless the name of my God with blessing,” he says, “and I will magnify him with praise.” It is not that he makes him great from a state of smallness; rather, he magnifies the benefactor whom unbelievers considered small: “I will make him great with thanksgiving.” Paul magnifies the giver of life: “Whether by life or by death, Christ will be magnified in my body.” Why does he magnify him? Because he cannot find the measure. Why would he magnify him? Because he cannot reach that honor with a human tongue. He magnifies not the nature of those being glorified, but the words of praise. I magnify Christ as much as I am able, not because I can speak in proportion to his greatness.

Just as those who worship God magnify him, so they also exalt him. “I will exalt you, my God and my King.” Surely they do not bring him up from lowliness to a higher position? What, then, does “I will exalt” mean? It is another way of saying, “I will proclaim your exaltation.” And because human nature is not sufficient, the divine Scriptures command, “Exalt the Lord our God,” for he is higher even than exaltation, and his exaltation is [?] measured by your glorification.

Therefore the three wise youths, who made the furnace a church and changed the flame into dew by the power of faith, blessed him to the best of their ability, and for what exceeded their ability, forgiveness [?]. They say, “All you works of the Lord, bless the Lord; bless him and exalt him above all forever.” They did not consider it sufficient to exalt him, but proceeded to exalt him still further, because they saw human weakness exposed by his surpassing greatness.

And here the three youths, exercising a certain watchfulness [?], bring all creation to worship. They mentioned the angels, the archangels, the powers, the waters, the sun, the moon, the rivers, the springs, the earth and its fruits, the sea and [?], the birds and livestock, the wild beasts and creeping things, and humankind. Among all these they introduced no mention of the Son, nor any word about the Holy Spirit, because the Son does not belong among those who worship, but among those who receive worship.

But perhaps someone will say, “How could the three youths bring the Son to worship, when they did not even know that he was the Son?” They did not know, because the prophets said nothing openly and plainly about the Son’s honor. But the name of the Holy Spirit was proclaimed through them. Although the name of the Son seemed unfamiliar to them, that of the Spirit was openly known. As Isaiah says, “They rebelled and angered the Holy Spirit”; and blessed David says, “Lord, do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

Consider the firm evidence: David and Isaiah did not live after the three youths, so that someone might say, “It was not known at that time, but was revealed afterward.” The three youths lived after David and Isaiah. Therefore they were acquainted with the writings of the prophets and knew that the Holy Spirit had been proclaimed. Why, then, do they bring all those creatures to worship, yet make no mention of the Spirit? They mention the angels, the archangels, the powers, and the others one by one, but do not mention the Spirit. For they saw him not joined with created beings, but revealed [?].

They themselves had been enlightened by the Holy Spirit, and, strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, they trampled the fire, like iron [?], or something that is refined into steel and tempered and becomes still harder and sharper. Likewise, when the souls of the righteous are tempered by the Holy Spirit, they regard fire as nothing, and water, the heavens, the earth, and everything within them.

But [?] those words, so that the disciples of the heretics may not regard them as groundless suppositions, [?] the statement of Paul, who recounts the Savior’s work of creation. The heretics perversely [?] this statement, because it says, “It came into being through him,” turning it upside down to demonstrate thereby some inferiority in the Son. In another place Paul does not say, “Through him,” but, “By him himself.” “By him,” he says, “everything was established, whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.” Pay close attention: “Whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.” So that he may not lead us into doubts and [?] stumbling, he enumerates the created beings, keeping the uncreated nature undefiled. “Everything,” he says, “came into being through him, whether thrones, dominions, or authorities.” And again: “Everything was established by him.” What everything? Thrones, authorities, dominions, rulers: everything was established through him and in him. And not only through him and in him, but by him and in him. And he is before everything, and everything was established by him.

And why did he leave out those other created things and not say, “The sun and the moon, heaven, earth, stars, and everything else”? Because it is quite evident that these visible things belong to the order of created beings; therefore he leaves out what is evident. And because among the invisible beings there are ranks of worshippers, while the uncreated nature receives worship, he considers it necessary to enumerate all those that are above the heavens, so that he may free the Holy Spirit from blasphemy and give the heretics no cause for rejoicing. “Everything,” he says, “came into being through him, whether thrones, rulers, authorities, or dominions.” And he did not say, “The Holy Spirit.”

And now they will ask: “How did the heretics arrive at that?” For they did not hesitate to pour out blasphemy against us in our weakness and fill every city with it, as though the Church preached three almighty beings. But I wished to persuade them once again not to blame us, but the prophets. If I were introducing words from my own thoughts and fashioning something novel against the truth, then they would rightly speak against me. But if we repeat the words of the prophets, the slander falls not upon us who explain them, but upon those who established the teachings. We have spoken not as they slanderously alleged, but as we believe. The Church recognizes not three almighty beings, but one power that holds everything. In truth, almighty power is recognized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Whoever says that there are three gods, separate from one another, let him be accursed. And whoever does not confess the Trinity as one almighty being, let him be accursed.

But do not consider these words strange or new when you see accusations of blasphemy heaped upon the truth; call to mind [?] the earliest saints. Stephen saw the heavens opened and the Savior at the right hand of God. He proclaimed what he saw, and because of his proclamation he was suspected of blasphemy. When that holy, loud-sounding trumpet declared, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,” the Jews could not bear the truth, but stopped their ears, as though blasphemy were being recounted rather than truth proclaimed. And do not consider it something new and strange if a true statement is thought to be blasphemy, for wickedness is accustomed to lay its own wrongdoing upon virtue. If we have embellished anything, we will be judged for that embellishment. If we have fashioned anything in a new form, we will have to give an account for fashioning it in a new form. But if the words of the prophets are being recounted, what fault is ours? Thus says the Lord Almighty: “Behold, I will come and dwell in your midst,” says the Lord, “and many nations will take refuge in you, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me.”

Why do you find fault with our words but not with those of the prophets? They boldly pronounce judgment in truth. Where there is truth, there is no fear at all; where there is faith, hesitation does not arise; where there is faith, there is strength; and where there is unbelief, there is hesitation. The Giver of Life said to the disciples, “Why are you fainthearted and have no faith?” Do you see? Where there is unbelief, there is faintheartedness, and where there is faith, there is strength. “Stephen,” it says, “full of faith and strength, performed great signs among the people.” And Paul says of Abraham, “He did not waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith.” I too boldly say that the name of the Father is also that of the Son. “Blessed,” it says, “is he who is to come in the name of the Lord”; and the Giver of Life says, “I came in the name of my Father.” Let us inquire what the Father's name is. The Scriptures proclaim “God” and “Lord” as the Father's name: “This is my name.” Pay close and steady attention: “I am,” he says, “the Lord God; this is my name.” If “Lord” and “God” are the Father's name, and I find the same name belonging to the Son, is it not evident that the Son is Lord and God? “Blessed,” it says, “is he who is to come in the name of the Lord. The Lord our God has appeared to us. Blessed is he who has come in the name of the Lord.” Therefore blessed Thomas, seeing that the Father's name is also that of the Son, and having received direct proof of the resurrection, cries out with a loud voice, “My Lord and my God!”

Let us see whether God has any other name in which the Son does not share. “Let them know,” he says, “that your name is Lord.” But when I say “share,” I do not mean by some gift of grace, but through a sharing in nature. David says, “Let them know that your name is Lord, and you alone are exalted over all the earth.” And the apostle says, “For us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” “One” and “alone” have the same force. The heretic assigns the name “God” to the Father and “Lord” to the Son. Since you have assigned “Lord” to the Son, and the prophet says, “Let them know that your name is Lord, and you alone are exalted over all the earth,” will you dare to say that there is one Lord and that Jesus alone is exalted, and not the Father? Consider how you will dare to say that Jesus is the one Lord when you hear from the prophet, “Your name is Lord, and you alone are exalted.” If you understand this as referring only to the Father, can you make the denial, “Jesus is not Lord”? And if you understand it as referring to the Son, can you, in turn, suppose that the Father is not Lord? Certainly not! Rather, let those words of yours agree with your thoughts, and do not call him Lord with your words while considering him a servant in your thoughts.

Would you call the Father Lord? “Yes,” he says. Would you also call the Son Lord? “Yes,” he says. Then how can you say there that he alone is Lord and Most High, and here that there is one Lord? Henceforth we must not count, but believe. If I call the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, you call me a believer in three gods. And if he calls the Father Lord and the Son Lord, what shall we call him? A believer in two lords, perhaps? Take note: you dare to speak of two lords, even if not in words, yet that is how you reckon in your mind. For you speak of one lordship belonging to the Father and another lordship belonging to the Son: one has unrestricted authority, and the other is subject to the Father’s lordship. If that is so, then there is not one Lord, nor does their lordship have one dignity and nature. You cannot call the two one Lord if the Father is Lord in one way and the Son is Lord in another. I wonder how you can serve a divided lordship, when the Lord himself says, “You cannot serve two masters.” But let us proceed to what lies before us. The Father is Lord and God; the Son is Lord and God, as has already been shown: “Let them know that your name is Lord,” and, “There is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Let us see whether we can find any other name for God in the Scriptures.

The blessed Moses says, “If the children of Israel ask me, ‘What is the name of the one who sent you?’ what shall I say?” See here too the blessed one who is to come in the name of the Lord. Take note of how he gives the true identifying signs: “You shall say, ‘He Who Is has sent me.’” If that is so, the Father’s name is “He Who Is.” Let us see whether the Son also has this same name; otherwise our defense is in vain. “He Who Is,” he says, “has sent me.” What are you saying to the apostle: “Whom am I to understand by ‘He Who Is’—the Father or the Son?” You are full of great foolishness when you ask, “The Father or the Son?” You divide their dignity; you do not recognize their union in equal honor [?]. Whom would you wish to call “He Who Is”? The one of whom the Scriptures spoke, the one whom I preached. Moses says “He Who Is” of the Father, and I say “He Who Is” of the Son: “I have sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart for my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, the giving of the law, the worship, the covenants, and the promises; to whom belong the patriarchs, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever.” Do you see that the Father’s name and the Son’s name agree with one another in words and in reality? “He Who Is has sent me.” “He Who Is over all, God blessed forever.” Is the expression somehow forced? Does it not indeed bear witness in reality [?]? Why do you condemn our words and despise the words of the prophets?

Let us consider another name [?] as well, for it was not said idly, “Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord.” Rather, every name belonging to the Father also belongs to the Son. The blessed Isaiah says to the people, “You have forsaken the Lord God your Savior, and you did not remember the Lord your Helper. Therefore you shall plant a faithless plant and faithless seed,” because you forsook God your Savior. Savior is a name of God; Helper is a name of God. Now let us see whether the Son is also Savior. Listen to the angels who praised him and brought good news to the shepherds. “We bring you good news of great joy,” they say, “for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord.” “You have forsaken God your Savior,” he says, “and you did not remember the Lord your Helper.” And where will you find the Son called Helper? A certain man, it says, came [?] and brought [?] his demon-possessed son to him. He says, “Kind Teacher, I brought my son to your disciples, and I could not heal him.” And the Savior says, “How long has it been?” Not so that he himself might learn, but so that those standing nearby might learn how long the affliction he was removing had lasted, and might benefit. “From childhood,” he says. “Often it throws him into fire and into water. I spoke to your disciples, and they could not heal him. But if anything is possible, help us.” Pay close attention: he accepted the man's approach, but rejected his approaching with a doubtful mind. If someone says to God, “If anything is possible,” that does not apply to God. Rather, the other statement applies: “All things are possible.” Since he approached him as though he were a prophet or an apostle possessing some limited power, able to do some things but unable to do others, the Savior then mocks his lack of understanding—or rather, instructs his foolish mind—because he said, “If you can.” And by his silence [?] he chastises his insolence. “All things,” he says, “are possible for the one who believes.” He makes nothing explicit in words, but the man standing nearby understood his anger from his face. When he saw that the Giver of Life was reproaching him and showing his anger in his face, what plea did the man who had erred cry out? “I believe, Lord,” he says. “Help my unbelief!” This was instead of saying, “I have erred; I did not know your power. Make up what I lack; help my unbelief.” For it was unbelief to say, “If you can, help.” But the father of the demon-possessed boy repented, while the misguided heretics, who often call upon the Son in their prayers, do not repent.

Oh, the foolishness! Write, if you will, that you do not regard the Son as equal in honor to God, nor the Spirit as equal in honor to the Son. Will you not regard them as equal in honor to the prophets? Have you not heard the words of the prophet Elijah? He says, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down and consume you, captain of fifty, and your fifty men.” The prophet commands with authority, but would the Lord of the prophets offer prayers? Elijah commands created things with authority, though he was not their lord, because his worship of God gave him confidence. There one could see a man of flesh commanding flashing fire and bringing fire down upon his opponents. Elsewhere the same blessed Elijah says to his disciple, “Ask something of me before I am taken up from you, and I will do it for you.” He did not say, “I will intercede,” but, “I will do it before I am taken up.” The prophets command with authority through the power of faith, yet you call the Lord of the prophets to obedience and consider yourself a partner in his prayers! Does not Joshua, who bears the Lord’s name, put you to shame? He stopped the sun without prayers. Did he say to the Lord, “Stop the sun”? Rather, he said with authority, “Let the sun stand still.” The servant had such power—or rather, it was the Lord’s name itself. For the sun did not stand in awe of him, but of the royal name. Will the Truth itself not perform acts of kindness with authority, but instead become an intercessor? But let us turn to the matter before us.

The Father’s name is “He Who Is,” and the Son’s name is “He Who Is.” The Father’s name is “Helper,” and the Son’s name is “Helper.” The Father’s name is “Almighty,” and the Son’s name is “Almighty.” If I speak merely by laying down a decree, do not accept it; but if I demonstrate it, do not reject it. Consider what you will [?] if you reject what I say. You insult the prophets; you deny God if you insult the prophets, and, advancing still further, you will fall into impiety. If you consider the words spoken by the prophets to be my own, you insult not me, their interpreter, but the utterances of the prophets and the action of God. Do you not know that God considers insults against the prophets to be directed against himself? When Samuel was rejected by the people, what did God say? “They have not rejected you,” God says, “but me.” And to make it clear that whoever does not listen to a teacher and a prophet does not listen to [?], he says to Ezekiel, “Son of man, go to the rebellious house and speak to them. They will not listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to me. If they listen to you, then they also listen to me; and if they listen to me, they also listen to you.”

It has already been shown that the Son is called Almighty. Yet another prophet also bears witness: “He who builds his ascents in heaven and establishes his good news on earth—the Lord Almighty is his name.” Who is it that built his ascents in heaven and established his good news on earth, if not the one who said to his disciples as he ascended, “I am with you until the end of the world”? Again: “Behold, I will come,” says the Lord Almighty, “and dwell in your midst.” What does “I will dwell” mean? The evangelist explains: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “Many nations will take refuge in the Lord, and you will know that the Lord Almighty sent me.” “Where,” they say, “is it written that the Son is Almighty?” Where is it written that the Father is Almighty? You demand words; I demand words. You collect evidence of power; I gather evidence of power. He spoke through the prophets; receive it from the prophets. “Search the Scriptures,” says the Savior. No one searches for what is already evident, but for what is hidden. “Search,” he says, “the Scriptures.”

See how the Trinity is proclaimed in the forms of a single authority. Listen to what he says: “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead the people astray.” Pay close attention: “They bite the proclamations with their teeth and speak peace with their mouths, yet he did not put peace into their mouths, so that no one would listen to the false prophets. But I,” he says, “will be filled; I will be filled with power through the Spirit of the Lord.” Either accept this and believe, or erase it from your thoughts, for you cannot erase the living Scriptures. “So that no one,” he says, “would listen to the false prophets. But I will be filled with power through the Spirit of the Lord.” He cannot say, “Through my own spirit,” but rather, “I will be filled with power through the Spirit of the Lord.” Who says this? Explain the words to me, so that I may understand the meaning of the power.

And elsewhere God says, “I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will stand against them in opposition. Yet I will have mercy on the children of Judah and will save them through the Lord their God.” Will you not save them through yourself, but through another God? The heretics do not understand that the words of the prophets are veiled. If he proclaimed things plainly, that would not be prophecy but proclamation; it would not be prophecy but gospel. Whatever is manifest is gospel, and whatever is wrapped up is prophecy. “And you, Daniel,” he says, “seal the words of this vision,” meaning, “Cover them with obscurity.” He does not mean, “Hide the writings,” which people read to this day, but the meaning of the words. The words of the prophets were sealed, and they are explained through the gospel.

Again God says to the people, “What shall I do with you? You have not accepted correction. I slaughtered your prophets with the sword of my mouth, yet even then you did not listen to me. I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” Why do you not say, “As I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” but instead, “As God overthrew them”? Have you, then, likened yourself to another? “I overthrew you,” he says, “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, yet even then you did not believe me.” Do you see the power concealed? Rather, he has illuminated it openly, before your eyes. Do you see the power of godliness boldly expressed?

Now why should you blame someone who calls the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit almighty? For example, when I say, “God and God and God,” I do not mean three gods, but one. Likewise, when I say, “Almighty and Almighty and Almighty,” I do not mean three almighty beings, but one. Let the voice of the Savior put you to shame. He said to the Jews, “It is written in your law that the testimony of two people is trustworthy.” When he says, “God and God,” do you not believe? Yet even when he says, “I and the Father,” he does not speak of two gods separate from one another, but of one divinity belonging to himself and the Father. He makes this clear in the other saying: “I and my Father are one.” He says “one” because of their inseparability, and “are” so that no one may regard the person as lacking distinct existence.

Let us care for our souls and [?]. Spit out that poison, wipe away the rust, scrape away the copper, and submit to him to whom even the demons submitted. Let changing circumstances teach you reverence. Do not be a believer in church and become a heretic when you go outside. Do not revere the word here and stray into brutishness when you go outside. A fickle soul does not remain settled amid changes or become steadfast. A God-fearing soul passes through changes but does not itself change. The worshiper of God worships God even in war, struggles bravely in famine, and does not grow slack in abundance. The worshiper of God is restrained and patient in everything and does not change with the changes of nature. The soul of a righteous person is neither shaken by the turmoil of wars nor made idle by an excess of ease. When right praise is proclaimed, that person is found eager to listen, and toward the obstinate, eager to be obstinate. Such a person does not depart from unity or have a divided mind.

There is one Lord God. Come, let us follow him. But if you follow error, you will arrive at error. Just as good wine is not harmed by changes—even if you transfer it from vessel to vessel, its taste and character remain the same—poor wine is quickly exposed by changes. Likewise, a God-fearing soul is not overcome by changes but overcomes change, while a shallow soul is quickly exposed. These are not my words but those of the blessed prophet Jeremiah, who cried out against the nation of the Moabites. For they had been at ease for a time and thought that they would enjoy ease [?], and they mocked Jerusalem's captivity. The prophet rebukes them: Do not boast of your ease or grow proud of your prosperity, for you have not yet undergone change. Your change too will come. He has not yet taken the matter in hand so that their intentions may be tested. And what does he say? Moab has been at rest from his youth and has not undergone the change brought by adverse circumstances. Moab has been at rest from his youth and has boasted in his glory; he has never been poured from vessel to vessel. This means that he has never gone into captivity. Therefore his taste remains in him, and his smell remains the same. Brothers, we must also bring forward the example from the divine teaching of the sealed holy Scriptures. For what does it mean to speak of the divinity of wine? Yet the prophet's teaching is unfailing salvation. Moab, he says, has been at rest from his youth and has boasted in his glory; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel and has never gone into captivity. Therefore his taste remains in him, and his smell remains the same. The Church was tested by adversity and poured from vessel to vessel: from peace into war and from war into peace. And a sweet fragrance remained in it. We are, he says, a sweet fragrance in Christ.

I have said all this, and I know that I have spoken at length. But since I have been slandered, I had to show that I was in the right, for this slander has spread throughout all the churches. Though one person spoke ill, everyone is indeed under reproach. I have answered on behalf of myself and the whole Church: the Church has one Lord, one God, one Creator, one Almighty, and one King. But when you hear “one,” think of God as the indivisible Trinity, of the endless and incorruptible kingdom, of glory and truth. It is never divided, [?] and remains eternal and life-giving. May all of us truly enjoy it and give glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
